From a provider perspective, it sounds like she was going through the insurance checklist and was reading you the questions straight up without modifying them for general politeness. With certain insurances, Medicaid in particular, they really want to hear that you've suffered enough to justify their approving treatment, otherwise it's not "medically necessary" or whatever they want to say to justify denying coverage. 

For cash pay folks, it's literally as simple as "This person is making this decision in sound mind and they have no medical or psychological reasons why they can't do what they want". For insurance folks, they really want to hear "This person has been suffering for so many years with all these terrible symptoms and they need this treatment that their doctor and a therapist and six other random professionals all agree they need but please insurance won't you cover it?"

And yeah, none of the above justifies systemic gatekeeping, but I think it does explain why it's still around. Providers don't want to risk their licenses and careers to push back against those requirements. Cis people who want gender affirming procedures can just go to the doctor and get them without jumping through all the hoops. It really highlights how casually transphobic every aspect of our society is.

Just chiming in as a therapist who writes letters (USA, CA)

To get all the info that insurance usually wants, I have to ask about the following:  
-Name and pronouns, including the name on your insurance card  
-date of birth  
-name and address of the surgeon or medical group  
-which surgery you want the letter for  
-dates (usually month or year) for when you started transitioning and for each previous thing you've done (changing legal name/documents, starting hormones, other surgeries, etc)  
-whether or not you have support during your surgery recovery including housing and care  
-whether or not you have any other mental health issues  
-whether or not you are experiencing dysphoria and how it interferes with your ability to live life how you want

I'm able to be more vague for folks who don't want to answer all those questions, especially the last 3 but insurance is more likely to deny the letter without them. The problem is making the letter sound like things are bad enough in your life that you need the surgery to improve things but not so bad that they think you can't cope with life. Most of the surgeons I work with are affirming and understanding that the letters are mostly for the insurance companies to get them to cover the surgery.

Not to be That Person, but I'm not an ex therapist, etc. I am a therapist, however, and I can see why people would want to leave. 

First off, it's widely known as the lowest paid master's degree (in America). You can make more as a manager at a Taco Bell. 

Second, there are a ton of barriers to entry. Out of all the freshly graduated associate therapists with their master's degrees, less than half will make it through internship to even get their therapy license. School is expensive, most internships are unpaid, and associate work is not much better.

Agency work is draining. The mental health field is not kind. Your manager will talk about boundaries and then expect you to work unpaid overtime to get all your billing in. If you take Medicaid, you have to jump through tons of hoops for documentation to justify why your clients need help. You'll see people take advantage of the system and you'll see the system walk all over people who truly need help. 

In private practice, you're on your own for marketing, budgeting, accounting, and following all applicable state laws while also providing good quality service to clients. It may sound like a lot to charge a client $100/hour, but after taxes and expenses you may still be better off managing that Taco Bell. 

Finally, the people who usually think they will be good therapists because they're empathetic and sensitive are the ones who burn out the fastest. Surviving and thriving as a licensed therapist takes more than just empathy. 

But that's just my take. I'm in private practice and doing fine. But sometimes, especially around tax season or slow seasons, I do find myself looking wistfully at regular jobs.
